source_adaptation: I16 timing retained: retrieval 5, input 7, guided analysis 10, increasingly independent application 13, reflection 5. H16 factors are addressed through fictional stories: redundancy and caring in A; health change, relocation and changing interests in B. Sensitive matters stay in the third person without diagnostic or personal detail. Extract useful strategies without portraying difficulty as deserved, necessary or automatically beneficial.
success: Order story stages and identify turning points.
Identify decision, setback, support and transferable skill with clues.
Explain at least two influences on the journey.
prepare: Books, pens, stories A/B, category guide, vocabulary and evidence record. Provide normal reading/scribing/typing aids. No prior lesson, visitor, internet, equipment or personal experience is needed. The stories are invented and unnamed. Keep the separate adult answer pages out of first responses.
activity: Retrieve skill transfer, model a story clue and effect, guide an annotated timeline, then independently analyse a fictional career journey. Explain two influences, support and transferable skills; give feedback and update Careers Portfolio/action plan.

evidence.description: Annotated career-journey case study: numbered stages and turning points; decisions, setbacks, support and transferable skills with story clues; at least two factors and their effects; a skill shown in its old and new tasks. Retain a useful strategy, realistic limit, normal access, answer prompts, first thinking and revision.

evidence_detail: Annotated career-journey case study: numbered stages and turning points; decisions, setbacks, support and transferable skills with story clues; at least two factors and their effects; a skill shown in its old and new tasks. Retain a useful strategy, realistic limit, normal access, answer prompts, first thinking and revision.
assessment: J16 annotated career-journey case study. Retain ordered stages and turning points; decision, setback, support and transferable-skill notes with clues; two factors and their effects. M16 asks for two factors influencing the journey. The exact outcome also requires all four categories. N16 F: formative; Spring 1 Week 6 is assessing.
boundaries: No names, real locations, employers, products or live sources. These are invented examples, not advice about individual health, employment rights or eligibility. Avoid blaming a worker for external barriers or presenting suffering as a required step to success. No learner history or future outcome is invented.
feedback: VF verbal feedback · WS worked with support · I independent · NS next step in green · // self-edit · ? read this back · E actual banked evidence · R after Voice, Audience, NS and a response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode.
response_modes: Book first. Optional Type instead has the same demand. Retain source label, first response, normal access, actual answer help and one revision. Offer to the Communication portfolio. E only for actual banked evidence; staff confirm any accredited mapping.

routes.Independent: Analyse B or compare it with A. Select precise stage clues, explain two influences and show a skill used before and again. Separate stated fact from a reasonable inference and keep a limit. A different evidence-based interpretation is welcome.
routes.Supported: Read one stage at a time. Use the category guide, numbered timeline, separate model and sentence frames. Rehearse a because link privately. Keep all four outcome categories and two influence explanations, then fade answer prompts where secure.
routes.Floor: Use A and the short choices. Read aloud or scribe the learner’s own thinking. Choose a category, then point to a story clue and give its effect. Sequence the four stages; identify all four categories and explain two influences through speech, scribe or usual aids. Choices alone are partial.

adaptations.Cognition and Learning: Use explicit instruction, modelling, guided practice and retrieval. Chunk each stage, keep category meanings visible and use a numbered timeline. Allow processing time and a checklist. Ask for one link at a time.
adaptations.Communication and Interaction: Pre-teach decision, setback, support and transfer. Offer private rehearsal, short frames and read-aloud support. Accept speech, typing, scribe or usual communication aids. No cold calling. Ask for the learner’s idea, not an adult-completed answer.
adaptations.SEMH: Explain the fictional nature of the stories. Do not ask about personal or family job loss, illness, caring or moves. Permit a pass, quieter response or regulation break with return. Use a trusted adult or the school’s help route privately if the topic is difficult.
adaptations.Sensory and Physical: Use clear print, numbered labels, normal aids and accessible seating. The lesson is reading and discussion only. Do not use colour alone to distinguish categories or outcomes; no physical repair task is required.
adaptations.EAL: Plan in any language. Pre-teach key words with concrete examples. Read a stage, pause, then check meaning. Separate language access from analysis. Normal aids continue while answer scaffolds fade.

hinge: “The shop role ended, so the worker must have worked badly.” A agree, or B the story says the business changed and gives no evidence of poor work? B. If any learner is unsure, separate stated fact from assumption, then use the parallel hinge.
parallel_hinge: “The worker starts a course, so a job is certain.” A agree, or B the course is a next step and the story states no job offer? B. If insecure, separate a planned action from a confirmed outcome and re-check another stage.
frames: Floor: “At stage ... , ... happened.” Medium: “This changed the route because ... .” High: “The story shows ... . This suggests ... , but ... is still unknown.” Skill link: “The worker used ... in ... and now uses it in ... .”
misconceptions: A career need not move in one straight line. A setback is not proof of poor character or effort. Resilience can include pausing, asking for support or changing a plan. Skills can transfer, but new tasks may also need learning. Support and opportunity vary; effort alone does not remove every barrier or guarantee a job.
ta_focus: Input: check category meanings. Guided work: point to a clue and ask for its effect. Independent work: preserve first thinking and record answer prompts. Prompt ladder: 1 point to place/instruction; 2 ask a short question; 3 rephrase; 4 provide scaffold/choice; 5 model the first step only, then return the task.
worked_example_and_fade: A stage 2: the business changes and the shop role ends. Mark this as a setback. The effect is that the worker must seek another route. Do not label it a choice or poor effort. Model the fact-to-effect link, jointly analyse stage 3, then let learners apply the categories to B.
check_after_model: Which is a decision: the business ends a role, or the worker chooses a shorter class? The class is the worker’s choice. The role ending is a setback in this story. Ask for the stage clue.

career_stories.title: Shop work to office learning
stages: A shop assistant checks orders and asks clear questions when details are missing. These skills help avoid mistakes.
The business changes and the role ends. This is redundancy. The worker has to look for another route. The story gives no sign that poor work caused it.
The worker has caring duties and cannot attend an all-day class. An adviser helps compare course times. A shorter class fits the hours available. The worker chooses it.
The worker starts an office course. They use clear questions and careful checks on a sample booking record. They plan to apply for office work. No job offer is stated.
career_stories.decision: The worker chooses a shorter office class after comparing its times.
career_stories.setback: The shop role ends because the business changes. The worker must seek another route.
career_stories.support: An adviser helps compare course times so the worker can consider a class that fits caring duties.
career_stories.transfer: Clear questions and careful order checks from shop work are used to check a booking record on the office course.
factors: The role ending creates a need to seek another route.
Available hours affect which class the worker can attend.
career_stories.strategy: Ask for advice, compare what is possible and take a manageable learning step.
career_stories.limit: The course is a next step, not a promised job. Class times, advice and other support may differ in real life.

career_stories.title: Stock work to repair learning
stages: A stock worker checks item codes against a list. They keep clear records and ask about a mismatch.
A health change means the worker pauses work. They need time and support to consider suitable work. The story gives no health details.
Later, the worker moves to another area. The old journey to work is no longer practical. An adviser helps compare local options and travel.
The worker finds an interest in repair work and chooses an introductory repair course. A tutor breaks learning into short steps and agrees time for questions.

On a paper repair plan, the learner checks a parts list and keeps a clear record. Skills from stock work help with this new task. The learner plans to ask about further training. No job or place is promised.
career_stories.decision: The worker chooses an introductory repair course after an interest in repair work develops.
career_stories.setback: A health change leads to a pause in work. The later move also makes the old journey impractical.
career_stories.support: An adviser helps compare options and travel. A tutor chunks learning and allows questions.
career_stories.transfer: Checking item codes and keeping records in stock work help with checking a parts list and recording a paper repair plan.
factors: The worker pauses and considers suitable work with support.
Moving makes the old journey impractical, so other options are compared.
Interest in repair work influences the course choice.
career_stories.strategy: Allow time, ask for help, review options and build on skills already used.
career_stories.limit: Support can help, but suitable work and courses may not be available. A change of direction does not guarantee a job.

story_status: Invented career stories prepared 30 October 2026. No real person, employer, place or course is described.
analysis_categories: Something that makes a plan harder.
Help, time or resources a person can use.
What help was given, and how did it help?
A skill that can be used in another task.
Where was it used before and where is it used now?
record_fields: Skill before and skill used again
private_help_route: Keep all case discussion in the third person. A learner may ask a trusted adult privately or use the school’s help route. Offer a pause, neutral task and agreed return if needed. Staff follow the usual school response if a concern is shared; do not seek disclosure or promise secrecy.

paragraphs_in_document_order: GROW · up to five learners · 40 minutes · formative lesson
Unit: Resilience & Change — Routes, choices & change
Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
I can analyse a career story and identify decisions, setbacks, support and transferable skills.
Weekly outcome: Students understand that career development includes change, setbacks, retraining and opportunity.

Source: specialist Careers scheme, GROW Careers physical row 16 / Spring 1 row 1. E16 intention; F16 focus; G16 outcome; H16 sequence; I16 timing; J16 evidence; K16 access; L16 support; M16 end check; N16 F.
How can a career change, and what can help a person take another step?
1. Put story stages in order and identify turning points. 2. Identify a decision, setback, support and transferable skill with story clues. 3. Explain how at least two factors influenced the journey.

Books, pens, stories A/B, category guide, vocabulary and evidence record. Provide normal reading/scribing/typing aids. No prior lesson, visitor, internet, equipment or personal experience is needed. The stories are invented and unnamed. Keep the separate adult answer pages out of first responses.

I16 timing retained: retrieval 5, input 7, guided analysis 10, increasingly independent application 13, reflection 5. H16 factors are addressed through fictional stories: redundancy and caring in A; health change, relocation and changing interests in B. Sensitive matters stay in the third person without diagnostic or personal detail. Extract useful strategies without portraying difficulty as deserved, necessary or automatically beneficial.
This helps me see more than one route, notice skills I can use again and ask for support when a plan changes.
Arrival prompt: a worker checks a shop order, then checks an office record. What skill could be used in both? Accept a clue; introduce transfer if new.
Teach career change and the four categories. Model A stages 1–2: fact, turning point and effect. Explain that a role ending is an event, not the worker choosing to fail.
Read A in stages. Order the timeline, discuss choices and support, and explain how redundancy and caring affect the route. Use hinge and fade the model.
Choose B, or A with support. Annotate the timeline and four categories. Explain two factors and an old-to-new skill link. Add a useful strategy and a realistic limit.
Check story evidence, give one NS and retain a short revision. Save the annotated journey in Careers Portfolio/action plan. Reflect on a useful strategy without disclosing personal events.
5 + 7 + 10 + 13 + 5 = 40 minutes. Chunk within each phase; use short pauses and agreed return points. Normal access continues as answer prompts fade.

Have the short shop/office prompt ready. “Checking details” or “asking a clear question” can transfer. This is a bridge from earlier skills work, not a prerequisite. A worker may need new learning as well as existing skills.

Use numbered stages and text labels so colour is not needed. Ask what happened, what the person chose, what help was available and what followed. A stage can involve more than one category; accept justified overlap. Keep sequence separate from cause.

In your book, write the story label and numbered stages. Add decision, setback, support and transferable-skill notes with clues. Write two because links for factors that changed the journey. Optional Type instead has the same demand. The sample future steps remain plans, not completed jobs.

Analyse B or compare it with A. Select precise stage clues, explain two influences and show a skill used before and again. Separate stated fact from a reasonable inference and keep a limit. A different evidence-based interpretation is welcome.

Read one stage at a time. Use the category guide, numbered timeline, separate model and sentence frames. Rehearse a because link privately. Keep all four outcome categories and two influence explanations, then fade answer prompts where secure.

Use A and the short choices. Read aloud or scribe the learner’s own thinking. Choose a category, then point to a story clue and give its effect. Sequence the four stages; identify all four categories and explain two influences through speech, scribe or usual aids. Choices alone are partial.

Use explicit instruction, modelling, guided practice and retrieval. Chunk each stage, keep category meanings visible and use a numbered timeline. Allow processing time and a checklist. Ask for one link at a time.

Pre-teach decision, setback, support and transfer. Offer private rehearsal, short frames and read-aloud support. Accept speech, typing, scribe or usual communication aids. No cold calling. Ask for the learner’s idea, not an adult-completed answer.

Explain the fictional nature of the stories. Do not ask about personal or family job loss, illness, caring or moves. Permit a pass, quieter response or regulation break with return. Use a trusted adult or the school’s help route privately if the topic is difficult.

Use clear print, numbered labels, normal aids and accessible seating. The lesson is reading and discussion only. Do not use colour alone to distinguish categories or outcomes; no physical repair task is required.
Plan in any language. Pre-teach key words with concrete examples. Read a stage, pause, then check meaning. Separate language access from analysis. Normal aids continue while answer scaffolds fade.

A stage 2: the business changes and the shop role ends. Mark this as a setback. The effect is that the worker must seek another route. Do not label it a choice or poor effort. Model the fact-to-effect link, jointly analyse stage 3, then let learners apply the categories to B.
Which is a decision: the business ends a role, or the worker chooses a shorter class? The class is the worker’s choice. The role ending is a setback in this story. Ask for the stage clue.

“The shop role ended, so the worker must have worked badly.” A agree, or B the story says the business changed and gives no evidence of poor work? B. If any learner is unsure, separate stated fact from assumption, then use the parallel hinge.

“The worker starts a course, so a job is certain.” A agree, or B the course is a next step and the story states no job offer? B. If insecure, separate a planned action from a confirmed outcome and re-check another stage.

A career need not move in one straight line. A setback is not proof of poor character or effort. Resilience can include pausing, asking for support or changing a plan. Skills can transfer, but new tasks may also need learning. Support and opportunity vary; effort alone does not remove every barrier or guarantee a job.

Floor: “At stage ... , ... happened.” Medium: “This changed the route because ... .” High: “The story shows ... . This suggests ... , but ... is still unknown.” Skill link: “The worker used ... in ... and now uses it in ... .”

Input: check category meanings. Guided work: point to a clue and ask for its effect. Independent work: preserve first thinking and record answer prompts. Prompt ladder: 1 point to place/instruction; 2 ask a short question; 3 rephrase; 4 provide scaffold/choice; 5 model the first step only, then return the task.

J16 annotated career-journey case study. Retain ordered stages and turning points; decision, setback, support and transferable-skill notes with clues; two factors and their effects. M16 asks for two factors influencing the journey. The exact outcome also requires all four categories. N16 F: formative; Spring 1 Week 6 is assessing.

Secure: a learner links redundancy to seeking another route, caring hours to class choice, advice to comparing times, and shop checking skills to the office task. Partial: labels without clues or effects, copied model with no understanding, only one influence, or naming a skill without showing its use before and again.

Keep all case discussion in the third person. A learner may ask a trusted adult privately or use the school’s help route. Offer a pause, neutral task and agreed return if needed. Staff follow the usual school response if a concern is shared; do not seek disclosure or promise secrecy.

No names, real locations, employers, products or live sources. These are invented examples, not advice about individual health, employment rights or eligibility. Avoid blaming a worker for external barriers or presenting suffering as a required step to success. No learner history or future outcome is invented.

Book first. Optional Type instead has the same demand. Retain source label, first response, normal access, actual answer help and one revision. Offer to the Communication portfolio. E only for actual banked evidence; staff confirm any accredited mapping.

VF verbal feedback · WS worked with support · I independent · NS next step in green · // self-edit · ? read this back · E actual banked evidence · R after Voice, Audience, NS and a response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode.

Spring 1 Week 1 · 4–8 January 2027 · Tuesday 5 January · P3

GROW Careers physical row 16 / Spring 1 row 1; E16–N16
Analyse invented career timelines; identify turning points, decisions, setbacks, support and transferable skills; explain two factors and useful strategies without romanticising difficulty.
Can the student identify two factors that influenced the career journey?
F source marker. Week 6 assessing. Independent / Supported / Floor. Normal aids and private responses; no cold calling.

I16 timing retained as 5/7/10/13/5. A covers redundancy and caring; B covers a health change, relocation and changing interests. Two complete fictional stories, numbered stages, guide, model, short choices and adult key. No real person, employer or place.

Keep sequence and cause distinct. A choice, setback and support may overlap at one stage if the learner explains why. Use stage clues to explain two influences and a skill used before and again. A planned course or application is not a job offer.
This helps me see more than one route, notice skills I can use again and ask for support when a plan changes.

No personal-disclosure prompts. Reader/scribe/typing, short chunks, visible model, word bank, private rehearsal and usual aids. Plan in any language. A learner may ask a trusted adult privately or use the school’s help route. Pause and return with support.

Keep the annotated case study in Careers Portfolio/action plan. Offer to the Communication portfolio. Retain actual help, first thinking, one NS and revision. E for banked evidence; R after Voice, Audience, NS and response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode.

I can analyse a career story and identify decisions, setbacks, support and transferable skills.

GROW Careers row 16 / Spring 1 row 1. E16 change/setbacks/retraining/opportunity; H16 timeline and sensitive change factors; I16 5/7/10/13/5; J16 annotated journey; M16 two influences; N16 F. Six-week Spring 1, Week 6 assessing.

A useful response identifies a stage clue and explains why it matters. A timeline shows order; analysis explains effects. The same stage can contain support and a choice. Accept justified overlap rather than forcing each event into exactly one category.

Model A stage 2 only: business changes, role ends, another route is needed. Then guide stage 3 and allow B or independent A analysis. Keep normal aids and reduce answer prompts when the learner can supply the clue and effect.

Use invented stories only. No personal or family questions about health, caring, redundancy or relocation. No diagnoses, treatment advice, employment-rights advice or job eligibility claims. Give a private route to a trusted adult or the school’s help route, with a pause and return option. Staff follow normal procedures for a concern, without probing for disclosure.

Support and opportunity differ. The worker is not responsible for every barrier. Do not imply hardship builds character, that staying positive solves structural barriers, or that every setback leads to success. Resilience may involve rest, help, new learning, a revised plan or stopping an unsuitable route.
Choose a shorter office class after comparing times.
Choose an introductory repair course after a changed interest.
Shop role ends after business change.
Health change causes pause; move makes old journey impractical.
Adviser compares course times with available hours.
Adviser compares options/travel; tutor chunks learning and allows questions.
Clear questions and order checks become checks on booking record.
Item-code checks and records become parts-list and paper-plan checks.
Redundancy creates need for another route; caring affects class timing.
Health change prompts pause; move changes travel; repair interest affects study choice.
Advice and manageable learning step; no job offer stated.
Time, help and skills reused; suitable work/training not promised.

A: “Redundancy affected the route because the role ended and the worker needed another option. Caring affected the class choice because the worker could not attend all day.” B: “The move affected the route because the old journey was not practical. Interest in repair affected the decision to take the course.”

Accept checking details, clear questions or accurate records where supported by the story. State the old and new tasks. “Team work” without a story clue is not enough here. A plausible added skill must be labelled an inference and explained; prioritise the given evidence.
Choosing the shorter class is the worker’s decision. The business ending the role is a setback. A worker can choose a response to an event without choosing the event itself.
B: the story describes business change, not poor work. If unsure, separate a stated fact, assumption and missing detail before the parallel hinge.
B: starting a course is a next step, not a guaranteed job. Re-check story A stage 4 or B stage 5.
A, A, B, A, B, A. Choice answers alone are partial. Retain stage order, four categories, clues, two influence explanations and a skill used before and again.

“They were resilient” gives no strategy. “They learned” gives no transferable skill. A timeline with labels but no effects is not full analysis. A course plan is not a confirmed place or job. Two examples of the same factor may not show two distinct influences.

Choose one: “Add the stage clue.” “Explain how that factor changed the route.” “Name the task where the skill was first used.” “Show the same skill in the new task.” “Separate a plan from a confirmed result.” Keep the learner’s first response and revision.

Ordered story stages with a turning point; decision, setback, support and transferable skill linked to clues; two factors explained through their effects. A useful resilience strategy and a realistic limit deepen the analysis. Do not require a positive ending or personal disclosure.

N16 formative. Record secure, partial or not yet against the actual response and support used. Reader/scribe/typing are normal access; adult answer supply is logged separately. M16 two factors does not replace the four-part exact outcome. Allow equivalent wording and justified overlap between categories.

Keep the annotated case study, story label, work reference, actual access and prompts, one NS and revision. Update Careers Portfolio/action plan. Offer to the Communication portfolio. E for actual banked evidence; R after Voice, Audience, NS and response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. Staff confirm any accredited mapping from actual work.

Tuesday 5 January 2027, P3, Year A. Spring 1 is six weeks, 4 January–12 February; Week 6 assessing. This return contains GROW Careers Week 1 only. BUILD RSHE Week 1 follows after Downloaded. The other Week 1 lines come before any Week 2 line. Separate later RSE topics remain outside this brief.
Story A Shop work to office learning
Invented career stories prepared 30 October 2026. No real person, employer, place or course is described.
A shop assistant checks orders and asks clear questions when details are missing. These skills help avoid mistakes.
The business changes and the role ends. This is redundancy. The worker has to look for another route. The story gives no sign that poor work caused it.
The worker has caring duties and cannot attend an all-day class. An adviser helps compare course times. A shorter class fits the hours available. The worker chooses it.
The worker starts an office course. They use clear questions and careful checks on a sample booking record. They plan to apply for office work. No job offer is stated.
Find a choice, a setback, some support and a skill used again. Say how two factors changed the journey. Use stage numbers as clues.
The course is a next step, not a promised job. Class times, advice and other support may differ in real life.
These are story events, not claims about all workers. Read and discuss only. No personal history or practical work task is needed.
Story B Stock work to repair learning
Invented career stories prepared 30 October 2026. No real person, employer, place or course is described.
A stock worker checks item codes against a list. They keep clear records and ask about a mismatch.
A health change means the worker pauses work. They need time and support to consider suitable work. The story gives no health details.
Later, the worker moves to another area. The old journey to work is no longer practical. An adviser helps compare local options and travel.
The worker finds an interest in repair work and chooses an introductory repair course. A tutor breaks learning into short steps and agrees time for questions.

On a paper repair plan, the learner checks a parts list and keeps a clear record. Skills from stock work help with this new task. The learner plans to ask about further training. No job or place is promised.
Find a choice, a setback, some support and a skill used again. Say how two factors changed the journey. Use stage numbers as clues.
Support can help, but suitable work and courses may not be available. A change of direction does not guarantee a job.
These are story events, not claims about all workers. Read and discuss only. No personal history or practical work task is needed.
Something that makes a plan harder.
Help, time or resources a person can use.
What help was given, and how did it help?
A skill that can be used in another task.
Where was it used before and where is it used now?
1. Put the stages in order. 2. Mark a point where the route changes. 3. Add a category and clue. 4. Explain the effect with because. 5. Show a skill used before and again.
A stage may fit more than one category. Give a reason. What happens next is not always caused by the event before it.
“At stage ... .” “The worker chose ... .” “This made the plan harder because ... .” “The help was ... .” “The same skill was used in ... and ... .”
Use a short pause, a reader, a scribe or your usual aid. Plan in any language. A private question to a trusted adult is always allowed.
At stage 2, the business changes and the role ends. This is a setback. It means the worker needs to seek another route. The story does not say that the worker did poor work.
The model shows a clue and an effect. Now look at class times, advice and the skill used again. Use your own words.
Use story A. An adult may read or scribe your choices.
A: Chooses a shorter class. B: The business changes.
A: The shop role ends. B: The worker asks a clear question.
A: A job is promised. B: An adviser helps compare times.
A: Checks orders, then a booking record. B: All tasks are the same.
A: It has no effect. B: It affects the class times that fit.
A: A job is still not confirmed. B: A course guarantees a job.
Choices alone are not the full task. Add clues and effects. Explain two influences and the skill before and after. Keep the story label.
Seek advice and compare another route.
A role ending does not prove poor effort.
Compare class times with time available.
A suitable class may not be available.
Pause and consider suitable work with support.
No health detail or treatment is given.
Moving does not promise a new job.
Try learning about another area of work.
New skills and entry checks may be needed.
Resilience can mean asking for help, taking time, learning or changing a plan. It does not mean ignoring a barrier or always coping alone.
Setbacks can be hard and can cost time or money. Support and opportunities are not the same for everyone. Effort can help, but it does not control every outcome.

Keep the discussion about the stories. You do not need to share a personal or family event. Ask a trusted adult privately or use the school’s help route if the topic is hard. You may pause and return with support.
Keep this page apart from first responses. Record the learner’s own thinking before giving the key.
A: Choosing the shorter class is a choice.
A: The role ending makes the plan harder.
B: Advice helps the worker compare class times.
A: Careful checking is used in two tasks.
B: Caring affects when the worker can attend.
A: The story gives no job offer.
Floor key A, A, B, A, B, A. Ask for a stage clue and an effect. Check all four categories and two factors. A category label or choice alone is partial.
Accept more than one category at a stage if the learner gives a sound reason. Keep fact and inference apart. A planned step is not a completed result. No need to share a personal setback.
A person’s journey through learning and work.
A route that changes direction rather than following one straight path.
An event or problem that makes a plan harder.
Help, time or resources a person can use.
A skill that can be used in another task or setting.
A point where the direction of a story changes.
A role ends because the job is no longer needed.
Learning skills for a different kind of work.
Responding to difficulty with time, support or a changed plan.
A detail that supports what you say.
An idea drawn from clues, not directly stated.
The story says ... . This affected the route because ... . The skill was used in ... and now in ... .
Plan in any language. Read, speak, type or use your normal aid. You can ask for help privately.

weekly_plan_row.objective_verbatim: I can analyse a career story and identify decisions, setbacks, support and transferable skills.
weekly_plan_row.evidence: Annotated career-journey case study: numbered stages and turning points; decisions, setbacks, support and transferable skills with story clues; at least two factors and their effects; a skill shown in its old and new tasks. Retain a useful strategy, realistic limit, normal access, answer prompts, first thinking and revision.
